newsitem.title: USA: U.S. power companies bank on overseas deals.
newsitem.headline: U.S. power companies bank on overseas deals.

text.p: A stagnant U.S. domestic market is forcing U.S. power companies overseas to beef up earnings momentum but potential rewards are matched by risks.
On Wednesday, Southern Co and AES Corp joined with a Brazilian investment fund to pay $1.06 billion for a 14.4 percent stake in Brazilian electricity utility Companhia Energetica de Minas Gerais.
"Returns in the U.S. are low and the market is so regulated that even the worst conditions overseas are better than here," said NatWest Securities analyst Edward Tirello.

Cemig is the latest deal in a series for both Southern and AES and comes just a week after Southern and Germany's Veba AG announced they would pay $1.9 billion for a stake in Berliner Kraft und Licht AG, the metro Berlin electricity supplier.
Southern's core business is growing at just two to two and a half percent a year, less than the U.S. economy as a whole.

"We aim to have 30 percent of our business outside our traditional business, and while some will be in domestic energy marketing, a significant part of that will be overseas," said Southern spokesman Chuck Griffin.
Southern's return on its core business is 12-13 percent and it is looking for more than that, noting that the Brazilian deal would be "immediately beneficial" to earnings.
The rationale behind the deals for the sellers is to tackle the non-payment problem for accounts which plagues state run utilities from Russia to Latin America.
Often the biggest debtors, as in the case of the former Soviet Union and Eastern Europe are state-owned companies and officials are reluctant to press for payment.
The key to getting any deal done is to get a local partner if you intend to be a long-term player.
Not all of the U.S. companies seen overseas currently are long term players, some are just using non-U.S. markets as a shelter while the domestic regulatory mess is cleared up.
"The big players in the overseas market, such as Southern, Duke Power Co and CMS Energy Corp, all go in with local partners and just get going," said Tirello.

For independent power producer AES, its latest deal is the third in the series of 10 projects the company set itself as a goal for 1997. It maintains the company's focus on Latin America, especially Brazil, where it owns a stake in neighbouring utility Light Servicos de Eletricidade SA.
What has changed throughout the world is that the economies which were once firmly wedded to either central planning or economic nationalism now embrace the free market.

AES is looking for a 16-20 percent rate of return in its new projects and is involved in Kazakhstan, where the risks of the businesses are highlighted by the problem of non-payment and the company is owed $25 million by the government.

"We knew it would not be easy, but the longterm potential is there and we are looking at swapping some of these debts into stakes in the regional electricity generators," said Ken Woodcock, senior vice president at AES.
While the companies acknowledge the risks, others note that there may be negative credit implications.
Most, including Southern and Duke Power use a downstream holding company to limit risks. In Duke's case an Argentine investment was written off by its Associated Enterprises Group subsidiary.

In the case of Southern, Moody's Investors Service credit analyst A. Tucker Hackett said that the $2.7 billion purchase of Consolidated Electric Power Asia and its use of commercial paper would be negative for the parent's P1 commercial paper credit rating until that were replaced with equity.

"The inability to pierce the corporate veil becomes important for bondholder protection. We view these investments as risky in the event of a crisis overseas and so carefully monitor the level of investment flowing down from the utility," she said. ((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
